chapter: Gene Mayl, Teddy Buckner and the Dixie Flies
title: Learning the slap-tongue and Yellow Dog Blues
summary: Joe slap-tongued on the spur of the moment in Santa Barbara, having been inspired by a twelve-year-old clarinetist years earlier, and Ory refused to record Yellow Dog Blues.

bands.name: Joe Darensbourg and His Dixie Flies

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: You had to juggle a bit here, slap-tongue it.
Yes.
Since you talk about "Yellow Dog Blues," I've forgotten to ask you about the slap-tonguing.
The first time I started doing the slap-tongue, which like you say was a lost art... At that time nobody did it.
Ain't nobody much does it now!

No. And I don't know why these things come to you. This tune, "The Sugar Blues," the trumpet would have a solo on it, and in the middle of it was a break. And I would take a low-register solo in "The Sugar Blues." So we was playin' a concert in Santa Barbara, and it just came to me, "When I get to this..." I had slap-tongued a little while before, just to see if I could do it. I had tried it. And when it come time for me to... Just on the spur of the moment, when I got to that break ([SINGS REFRAIN], or something like that it went), heh-heh, I slap-tongued it. And everybody, man, in the house just started applauding.
Darensbourg - 215
Where did you learn that from? Who did you see do it at first?
Well, I used to see a few clarinet players. I can't remember too many guys doing it.
Willie Humphrey used to do it.
Yeah.
I've seen Willie do it. In fact, that guy asked us the other day 'Who else did you see do it?' -- and I forgot about Willie.

But really, what made me want to do it, to learn how to do it... I run into a little 12-year-old kid when I was working for those gangsters -- to make a long story short, and come back a little. His name was Harry. I was at his sister's house to have dinner, and she's a piano player. When you're on one of them shows, you're always looking for a free meal, you see. I don't know if I've told you this before.
No.

So this gal's name was Lucille, and she was playing a piano and we was playing 'Let Me Call You Sweetheart' or something. He says, 'I got a little brother who plays clarinet. Would you like to hear him play?' I said, 'Sure!' Twelve years old. And here he come in the room with that darn clarinet... They had an old tune called
Darensbourg - 216

"Don't Bring Me Poses, 'Cause Shoes Is What I Need"...was the title of it. It's a Blues number. "Don't bring me poses, shoes is what I need..." And this little sucker picked up that clarinet and started playing it, [SINGS SLAP-TONGUE]... He stopped playing, I said, "Lord have mercy!" But I couldn't stop thinking about it.
But had you see anybody else years ago do it?

I did a little of it, but it... Oh yeah, I seen it! It wasn't too many guys did it, as I can remember. Maybe one or two. Most everybody that did slap-tongue... I don't ever remember a clarinet player doing it. A lot of the saxophone players used to...some of them used to do it. But anyway, when this darned little old kid did that, then his sister turns around to me and says, "Ain't that good, my little brother Harry? Can you do that?" I says, "Of course I can do it. I didn't want to act dumb." And she says, "Let's see you do it." Then all of a sudden I started getting a toothache and a headache and everything, and I said, "I really don't feel... I can do it, but I don't feel up to it." And finally, she kept egging me on about doing it, and they made me mad, and I walked out of the house -- missed my dinner and everything. But I vowed right then and there that I was going to slap-tongue. And then I developed it. I really learned how to do it.
Darensbourg - 217
Well, that made that "Yellow Dog Blues" such a hit.

So when Ory first started playing "Yellow Dog Blues," it was a natural because of...[SINGS REFRAIN] So I figured to start that thing in the low register with a slap-tongue, it would sound good. Ory didn't think much of the idea, but anyway, we did it. And every time we would do that, we would get a terrific hand. And when it came to record, Ory never... Ory said, "Aw, I ain't gonna record that thing. It never would go." So I made up my mind right then and there, if I ever get a band and to record a session like that, that I'm going to record that tune.
